To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the time of deterministic broadcast is Θ(r + log n + log Δ) if the source knows r,  (2) the time of broadcast is Θ(r) if the source does not know r,  (3) the time of multicast is Θ(r + (log Δ)/log log n + (log n)/log log n) if the source and the receivers know r, and  (4) the time of multicasting is O(r + log n)
the deterministic broadcasting time in the one-way model with partial knowledge is Θ(r) and that the deterministic broadcasting radius is Θ(r) for any r.

the broadcasting time of a network is at most 2r+2Δ−2+1 rounds if the knowledge radius is at least 1, and at most 3r+Δ+2 rounds if the knowledge is radius 0 (i.e., if each node knows only its neighbors).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the time of broadcasting in networks where each node has only limited information on the network, i.e., the part of the graph that it can see.
the time required to broadcast in networks whose nodes know only a small fraction of the topology, and in which each node can communicate only with its immediate neighbors in each round.
the time of deterministic message broadcasting in networks whose node knowledge is restricted to a small part of the network, and we present the first results on the topic.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the time of deterministic broadcast is Θ(r) in networks whose nodes know only r, Δ, and n.
there are many different approaches to solve the broadcasting problem in networks with different assumptions on the network topology, on the communication model and on the knowledge of the nodes.
there is an upper bound of O(n) rounds and a lower bound of Ω(√ n) rounds for the deterministic broadcasting time of the one-way model with partial knowledge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how to achieve deterministic broadcasting in time O(r + Δ + log n).
we provide a complete characterization of the time of broadcasting for all r, Δ, and n.
we give a tight lower bound of Ω(r + Δ) for broadcasting time and an algorithm that achieves this bound.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in spite of the limited knowledge, we can design broadcasting algorithms that are almost optimal.
the time of deterministic message broadcasting can be significantly reduced when the knowledge radius r of the nodes increases.
the knowledge of the network topology, even when it is very limited, can significantly improve the time of deterministic broadcast in a network, even if the network is not known to be connected.
